title: Largest Perimeter Triangle
description: Brute force to optimized: checking every triple versus sorting descending and scanning only adjacent triples.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given an array of integers representing side lengths, return the largest perimeter of a triangle that can be formed using three of these lengths, or 0 if no valid (non-degenerate) triangle can be formed. Three lengths a <= b <= c form a valid triangle if a + b > c.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","nums, an array of positive integer side lengths"],["Output","The largest valid triangle perimeter, or 0 if none exists"],["Goal","Find this via sorting and checking adjacent triples, avoiding checking every combination"],["Constraints","3 <= nums.length <= 10^4"]]}

{"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"Largest perimeter satisfying the triangle inequality\"","Sort descending; the largest values are the best candidates to check first"],["Triangle validity only depends on the two SMALLER sides summing past the largest","Checking adjacent triples in sorted order is sufficient, no need to check all combinations"]]}

blocks.text: For three sorted lengths a <= b <= c, they form a valid triangle exactly when a + b > c. Sorting all lengths descending and checking consecutive triples (starting from the largest) finds the FIRST (and therefore largest possible) valid triangle quickly, since any valid triple found this way uses the largest possible values available.

blocks.title: Analogy: Finding the Largest Usable Set of Three Rulers
blocks.text: Picture a collection of rulers of different lengths, wanting to pick three that could form a triangle (any two shorter ones must together exceed the longest) while maximizing the total length used. Sorting rulers from longest to shortest and checking the largest three first, then sliding down if they do not work, quickly finds the best usable set.

blocks.caption: Sorting descending and checking adjacent triples finds the largest valid triangle directly

blocks.text: Result: 5. Sorted descending: [2,2,1]; 2 < 2+1, so this triple is valid, giving perimeter 5.

Before checking every possible triple of side lengths, notice that sorting descending and checking ADJACENT triples suffices: if the two smaller of the current largest three do not exceed the largest, using any EVEN SMALLER values instead would only make the inequality harder to satisfy, so skipping past the current largest value (rather than trying non-adjacent combinations) is safe.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: For a sorted triple a <= b <= c, validity requires only a + b > c, the tightest constraint being between the two smallest values and the largest.

Observation 2: If the current largest three values (sorted) do not form a valid triangle, replacing the LARGEST of them with a smaller value cannot help, since a smaller largest value only makes the inequality a+b>c HARDER to violate in the wrong direction, actually wait, it makes it EASIER to satisfy since c decreases; but any valid replacement must still involve the two next-largest remaining values as candidates for a and b, which is exactly the next adjacent triple.

Observation 3: This means scanning sorted (descending) triples in adjacent groups of three, moving one step at a time, correctly checks all PROMISING candidates without needing non-adjacent combinations.

Observation 4: The first valid adjacent triple found (starting from the largest values) gives the largest possible perimeter, since any triple found later in the scan uses strictly smaller values.
This leads to sorting descending, then scanning adjacent triples from the largest values downward, returning the first triple satisfying the triangle inequality.
Check every possible triple of side lengths directly, tracking the maximum valid perimeter found.

items: For every triple of indices (i, j, k), check if the three lengths satisfy the triangle inequality.
If valid, compute the perimeter and track the maximum found.
Return the maximum valid perimeter, or 0 if none exists.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Checking every triple directly implements the definition, guaranteed correct.
This costs O(n cubed), unnecessary once sorting reduces the check to adjacent triples only.

blocks.text: Limitation: sorting descending and checking only adjacent triples finds the largest valid perimeter in O(n log n) instead of O(n cubed).

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why checking every triple is unnecessary: once sorted descending, if the current three largest values fail the triangle inequality, no triple involving the CURRENT largest value could ever succeed either (since it would need even larger partners, which do not exist further left), so it can be permanently discarded.

The adjacent-triple scan: after sorting descending, check nums[i], nums[i+1], nums[i+2] for each i in order; the FIRST one satisfying nums[i] < nums[i+1] + nums[i+2] gives the largest possible perimeter.

Why non-adjacent triples never need checking: any non-adjacent choice would use a strictly smaller sum than the corresponding adjacent triple at the same starting position, so it could never produce a LARGER valid perimeter than what adjacent scanning would find first.

The core idea: sort descending, scan adjacent triples, return the first valid one.
Sort nums descending. Scan i from 0 to n-3, checking if nums[i] < nums[i+1] + nums[i+2]; return their sum as soon as this holds. If no such triple is found, return 0.

blocks.caption: Sort descending, scan adjacent triples, return the first valid one

blocks.text: After sorting descending, if the three largest remaining values fail the triangle inequality, the current largest value cannot form a valid triangle with ANY other two values either, since those would need to sum to more than it, but no two LARGER values remain. Discarding it and moving to the next adjacent triple correctly and efficiently finds the first (and therefore largest-perimeter) valid triple.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n log n), dominated by the sort.
Space: O(1) extra (or O(n) if the sort is not in-place).

blocks.text: Largest Perimeter Triangle is a clean example of "sort, then only adjacent elements matter," since the triangle inequality's binding constraint is always between the two smallest and the largest of a sorted triple.

items: Using a non-strict inequality (>=) instead of strict (>) for the triangle validity check.
Checking non-adjacent triples unnecessarily, missing the insight that adjacent triples alone suffice.

blocks.text: Explicitly justifying WHY adjacent triples suffice after sorting (the discarded largest value cannot pair validly with any two remaining values either) shows precise understanding of the greedy argument's correctness.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "largest/best selection satisfying a pairwise inequality among three sorted values", think: sort, then only adjacent elements need checking.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Checking every triple costs O(n cubed) time; sorting descending and scanning adjacent triples costs O(n log n) time, both using O(1) extra space.

items: Pattern: sort, then only adjacent elements need checking, since the triangle inequality's binding constraint is local in sorted order.
Core Idea: sort descending; return the first adjacent triple satisfying a < b + c.
Time: O(n cubed) for checking every triple, O(n log n) for the optimized sort-and-scan.
Most Important Observation: if the largest three values fail, the largest value can never form a valid triangle with anything, so it is safely discarded.
Interview Difficulty: an accessible greedy problem built on the classic triangle inequality.
One line memory trick: sort descending, check adjacent triples, return the first valid one.
